prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated together to reach a fractional uncertainty near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B041 as my preferred configuration after reading the whole first-round exchange. The chair asked whether a citation can be written that separates the lattice clock from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of individual quantum systems. I think it can, and the wording above does it: the discovery is a scheme, not a general improvement in timekeeping. Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes the lattice light shift on the clock transition, which allows many neutral atoms to be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated in parallel. That is a different route from single-ion control, and it is what made stability and systematic uncertainty at the 10^-18 level accessible. Ye's work took the performance to that limit and showed that many-body effects in the atomic ensemble matter for the clock. The result is reproduced and intercompared by several national and university laboratories, and it is already used for tests of constants, dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy. The two-name credit is complete in the sense that matters: the originator of the scheme and the leading experimentalist, with no decisive contributor squeezed out by the three-person cap. Decisively for me, the evidence is mature and the interpretation is not in dispute, which is not true of B030, and the credit does not have the open attribution problem that colleagues agree B018 and B020 carry.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against B041 is the one Danielsson and Eriksson make: a new class of matter and a new organising principle for band insulators have a wider conceptual reach than a measurement technology, and precision timekeeping has been honoured in 2005 and 2012. I also accept that the pending redefinition of the second is not yet decided, and that ultrastable-laser work and ion clocks, which sit outside the two names, made the comparisons possible. If the committee judges that a measurement regime is not a discovery in the sense of the will, or that the field is occupied, B018 is the better choice, and I would support it without reservation about the science. What separates the two for me is attribution, not merit. A prize that must explain in its own citation why Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not included is more exposed than one with no such omission, and I would not set conceptual reach against a complete credit by default.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B018 first on the grounds that a symmetry-based prediction followed by decisive observation reorganised how condensed-matter physicists classify band structures, and asks whether the decisive step in B041 is the lattice scheme or the later metrological performance.
responses.response: The lattice scheme and the performance cannot be separated as cleanly as that. The magic wavelength is a necessary condition for reaching the performance, since without it the trap shifts the transition by far more than the target uncertainty, and Ye's evaluations showed that the scheme actually delivers it and that collective effects among the atoms had to be understood and controlled. So the decisive step is the scheme turned into a working clock, and I would write the citation that way. I accept that your point on conceptual reach is a real difference of kind between the two candidates, but reach into other fields (geodesy, dark-matter searches, constants) is also concrete here. On B018 I would still support the narrowed quantum spin Hall citation, but my view of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap is that it is a more serious obstacle than your reading allows, because the experiment was designed from their proposal.

responses.point: Kroll shares the B041 first choice, stresses that the increment over 2005 and 2012 is a new accuracy regime reached with many neutral atoms, and says the contributions of ultrastable-laser work and ion clocks are best handled in the citation wording, not by adding names.
responses.response: I agree and I take your point that the citation is where the precedent question gets decided. I would add that the committee should state in its deliberation that the ultrastable-laser and ion-clock work enabled the comparison but is not the claim being recognised. Your disclosure of a stay in Hall's laboratory is decades old and documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye, so I do not think it affects your judgement. As you do, I treat the redefinition of the second as neutral: the physics is established independently, so it is not a reason to wait.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B018 from B016, calls B041 the strongest competing case because of its clean two-name credit, and says he would move to B041 without hesitation if the committee finds the B018 attribution problem disqualifying.
responses.response: That is the criterion I think should decide between the two, and I would put it in terms of what a citation can honestly say. For B041 the citation says what was invented and by whom, and nothing relevant is left outside the names. For B018 a narrowed quantum spin Hall citation can be defended, but the committee would need to explain a real omission. I do not call that disqualifying. I would move to B018 if the committee decided a measurement technology cannot be a discovery in the sense of the will, and I think you and I are close on this. Where I differ from you is that I do not think B018's two decades of confirmation outweighs the cleaner credit of B041, because B041 has also been confirmed independently and for more than a decade.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B018, citing the pairing of theory and experiment, two decades of reproduction in 2D and 3D systems, and the way first-principles searches for topological materials changed band-theory practice.
responses.response: I accept that the change in practice is real, and it is the strongest evidence of impact for B018. The claim of impact in B041 is of a different kind, a shift in what can be measured, with consequences in other fields. I do not think either is more important in a way that the committee can decide on. On the 2016 prize, my reading is closer to yours than to the sceptics': the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class is a separate discovery from the quantum Hall and chain physics honoured then. So the 2016 prize is not my reason for preferring B041. My reason is that a narrowed citation still leaves the HgTe proposal unrecognised, and the experiment cannot be presented as following Kane and Mele directly.

responses.point: Lindroth shares B041, argues the citation should be anchored on the lattice and magic wavelength rather than on generic metrology, and observes that no pairing of B041 with a second shortlisted part fits within three people.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and on the single-part configuration. I looked at whether a second part could be added within the three-person limit and could not find one that does not force an exclusion in the other candidate. A prize for B041 alone is also easier to defend than a diluted pair. Your note about possible proximity to B020 through ETH Zurich is relevant only to a candidate I have already set aside, so I do not think it needs further action.

uncertainties: Whether a majority of the committee will accept a measurement technology and its performance as a discovery in the sense of the will, given the 2005 and 2012 precedents, or will treat it as an evolutionary step.
Whether the narrow quantum spin Hall citation for B018 can be defended against the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission; if the committee judges so, B018 may rightly lead, and I would not oppose it.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be read as a reason to act now or to wait; I believe the physics is already established, but the committee may weigh it differently.
I rely on memory for priority details of the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock demonstrations, and these should be checked against the primary papers.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. B020 lies in my own field: I direct WACQT at Chalmers and work on superconducting circuits and circuit QED, I know several of its researchers professionally, and Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work in the area. I would recuse myself from any final decision on B020, and it is no longer among my alternatives. I disclose no specific connection to B041, B018 or B030 from my profile.
